premise: The sharpest observation in the source material is not any single citation: it is that these references belong to communities that normally publish separately, and that the bridge is the unusual part of the project. A bibliography cannot show that, so every entry carries its community and the ladder rung it serves, and the bridges are computed from those two fields rather than claimed.
provenanceNote: Two classes, and the distinction is not pedantry. `public-artifact` covers a library, standard, database or paper whose existence and purpose are common knowledge in its field — BLIS, GraphBLAS, TACO, MLIR, GROMACS, PDB, OMIM, Turing 1952. `author-supplied` covers claims about PEOPLE, POSTS, PROGRAMMES AND MONEY: who works where, who sits on which board, which programme holds which grant. This repository has verified none of the second class and no file in it resolves a single one. Publishing them unmarked beside the first class would launder one into the other.

communities.name: Rare-disease biology and therapy
communities.note: The people who would actually treat someone. Publishes in medical genetics and neuro-oncology venues.

communities.name: Rare-disease infrastructure
communities.note: Ontologies, registries and variant catalogues. Rarely credited as research and load-bearing for all of it.

communities.name: Systems and computational biology
communities.note: Networks, single-cell, spatial, structure, dynamics. Publishes in bioinformatics and systems-biology venues.

communities.name: High-performance and sparse computation
communities.note: Numerical linear algebra, graph algorithms, profiling. Publishes at SC, PPoPP, IPDPS — venues the biology communities do not read.

communities.name: Compilers and runtimes
communities.note: IRs, lowering, kernel generation, domain-specific compilation. Publishes at PLDI, CGO, ASPLOS.

communities.name: Complex systems and morphogenesis
communities.note: Named by the author as influence rather than as a discipline being bridged, and kept that way here.

references.name: Krizelle Alcantara

references.name: Brian Kaspar
references.why: Historical reference for CNS gene therapy; the environment the SMA strategies came out of.

references.name: Terry Flotte
references.why: AAV, gene replacement and silencing in monogenic disease.

references.name: Katharina Meijboom
references.why: Associated with the experimental NF2 gene-therapy lines.

references.name: John Mekalanos
references.why: Bacterial immunotherapy against NF2 tumours — engineered attenuated Salmonella.

references.name: Elisabeth Castellanos
references.where: Germans Trias i Pujol Research Institute (IGTP)
references.why: Patient-specific antisense oligonucleotide strategies — the concrete European route into N-of-1 therapeutics for a private variant.

references.name: Marco Giovannini
references.why: Murine models of NF2, including the historical lines. The reference behind the author's point that the animal should follow the prioritisation.

references.name: Lei Xu
references.why: Preclinical models of NF2.

references.name: Helen Morrison
references.why: Merlin biology and the cellular mechanisms of its loss — the European anchor for the molecular half rather than the tumour half.

references.name: Cure NF2 Foundation
references.why: A portfolio rather than a single bet: gene addition, a suicide-gene programme, bacterial immunotherapy, a biobank, preclinical models, microenvironment work. The author records raised funds, programme counts and a biobank size; none is verified here.

references.name: Children's Tumor Foundation
references.why: Works across the neurofibromatoses and schwannomatoses and functions as the bridge between researchers, patients, industry and trials.

references.name: NIH / NINDS
references.why: The funder of record for the neurological half, including the SBIR mechanism the author cites for one programme.

references.name: GeneReviews — NF2-Related Schwannomatosis
references.why: The clinical baseline: genetics, phenotype, diagnosis, natural history, management.

references.name: ClinVar
references.why: Variant-level clinical interpretation with review status. The genotype rung of this project stops at genes; this is where variants would enter.

references.name: COSMIC
references.why: Somatic mutation catalogue. NF2 is germline AND somatic, and the architecture has to keep the two apart.

references.name: OMIM
references.why: Gene to Mendelian phenotype. Already one of the three identifier spaces this atlas joins, and the reason its disease count is larger than the usual 7,000-8,000.

references.name: Human Phenotype Ontology
references.why: A patient becomes a set of terms rather than free text, and phenotype similarity becomes computable. Already ingested here, and the source of the inheritance measurement behind the non-gene tab.

references.name: Orphanet
references.why: Rare-disease classification, epidemiology, orphan drugs. Already ingested — and its CC BY-ND licence shaped this repository's architecture.

references.name: Monarch Initiative
references.why: Integrates genes, diseases, phenotypes and model organisms. The closest existing thing to the knowledge graph the thesis describes.

references.name: N-of-1 antisense therapeutics
references.why: The paradigm case that changed how the field discusses treatment when N = 1. The logical extreme of the thesis's own architecture.

references.name: Albert-László Barabási
references.why: Network medicine: disease as a perturbation of a module in a molecular network rather than a property of one gene. The scientific school closest to the thesis's second insight.

references.name: BioGRID
references.why: Curated protein-protein interactions — the concrete substrate for a Merlin subgraph and the propagation on it. Named in this project and not ingested.

references.name: STRING
references.why: Scored functional associations, decomposed by evidence type. Denser than BioGRID and requires a threshold, which is a judgement to state rather than inherit.

references.name: KEGG
references.why: Pathways, metabolism, gene networks — and a source of real biological graphs for benchmarking sparse kernels.

references.name: Reactome
references.why: Curated pathway membership. Would turn this project's hand-written Hippo gene list into a citation.

references.name: Protein Data Bank
references.why: Experimental structures. The step before trusting any prediction of Merlin.

references.name: AlphaFold
references.why: Predicted structure at proteome scale — with the caveat the thesis states itself: a predicted structure is not protein dynamics.

references.name: ESMFold
references.why: Fast structure prediction from a language model; the benchmark against AlphaFold rather than a replacement for it.

references.name: Rosetta
references.why: Structure, design, docking, and the ddG of a mutation.

references.name: FoldX
references.why: A second, independent estimate of mutational ddG — the point being not to depend on one method.

references.name: GROMACS
references.why: Molecular dynamics. Where structure becomes an ensemble, and where the sampling bottleneck actually bites.

references.name: Emulators of conformational ensembles
references.why: The new generation trying to cut the cost of conformational sampling with learned models — aimed exactly at the question of how a mutation moves a distribution of states rather than a single structure.

references.name: GEO
references.why: Expression datasets, including single-cell — the concrete route to schwannoma cell-state data.

references.name: TCGA
references.why: Cancer genomics at scale; useful for transfer between tumours rather than for NF2 directly.

references.name: 10x Genomics datasets
references.why: Public single-cell matrices — over 90% sparse, and therefore a workload as much as a biological resource.

references.name: Scanpy / AnnData / Seurat / scvi-tools / CellRank / PAGA
references.why: The single-cell stack. PAGA in particular is graph computation over cells, which is the thesis's point that cellular biology already IS graph computation.

references.name: Visium / MERFISH / Slide-seq / Xenium / SpatialData / Squidpy
references.why: Spatial transcriptomics: cell, gene, x, y, neighbourhood. Produces exactly the large sparse neighbourhood graphs the computational thesis is about, and it is the emptiest rung in this repository.

references.name: CRISPR perturbation screens
references.why: Observations closer to interventions than to correlations — the reason the DepMap adapter is the one this library was hardened against.

references.name: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier
references.why: Historical reference for the editing chemistry. What matters to this thesis is downstream: screens, Perturb-seq, base and prime editing, variant validation.

references.name: Perturb-seq
references.why: CRISPR plus single-cell readout: perturbation in, transcriptomic response out. The experimental version of what the thesis wants a model to learn.

references.name: Aydın Buluç
references.where: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory / UC Berkeley
references.why: GraphBLAS, sparse matrix algorithms, SpGEMM. The principal reference for the BioSparse line.

references.name: GraphBLAS
references.why: Graph algorithms expressed as sparse linear algebra. The formal equivalence that connects biological graphs to hardware.

references.name: Timothy A. Davis
references.why: SuiteSparse and SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS. Any own implementation of sparse computation is measured against this ecosystem or it is not measured.

references.name: SuiteSparse and its Matrix Collection
references.why: The reference implementation and the reference benchmark set. The planned comparison was SuiteSparse's general families against BioGRID, STRING, KEGG and single-cell.

references.name: Erin Carson
references.why: Numerical linear algebra, communication-avoiding algorithms, mixed precision.

references.name: Helen Xu
references.why: Sparse linear algebra and HPC; recorded as a potential intellectual contact once there is a concrete experimental result to discuss.

references.name: Robert van de Geijn
references.why: The pedagogical route into GEMM: naive, loop order, tiling, packing, register blocking, SIMD.

references.name: Kazushige Goto
references.why: Co-author of Anatomy of High-Performance Matrix Multiplication — why fast GEMM is organised around cache blocking, packing, microkernels and register reuse.

references.name: Field G. Van Zee
references.why: BLIS, which makes the architecture of GEMM explicit and extensible rather than hidden behind an interface.

references.name: BLIS
references.why: The framework the author's HPC track was built around.

references.name: BLAS and LAPACK
references.why: The historical substrate, and the origin of the author's question: what if an abstraction at this level knew something about the semantic structure of the data?

references.name: OpenBLAS
references.why: The CPU baseline. The pedagogical goal was a meaningful fraction of it before touching sparse work at all.

references.name: cuSPARSE
references.why: The baseline for the BioSparse hypothesis — and the author's own correction: the defensible question is not beating a general kernel everywhere, it is beating it on specific structural subclasses of biological graphs.

references.name: CUTLASS
references.why: Modern GPU GEMM kernels, to be studied rather than reinvented.

references.name: Ginkgo
references.why: Sparse linear algebra for accelerators, and a well-structured codebase to read.

references.name: GraphBLAST
references.why: GraphBLAS on the GPU: graph analytics, sparse matrices and accelerators meeting.

references.name: Sputnik
references.why: Sparse kernels built for deep learning — an architectural reference for highly specialised sparse computation.

references.name: Nsight Compute and Nsight Systems
references.why: Because the thesis cannot be judged on runtime alone: memory transactions, cache behaviour, occupancy, warp divergence and stall reasons are the evidence.

references.name: Intel VTune
references.why: The CPU half of the same argument: cache misses, branching, threading.

references.name: Tensor Cores and 2:4 structured sparsity
references.why: Structure that is incorporated physically into the hardware — the existence proof that a sparsity pattern can be worth silicon.

references.name: MLIR
references.why: Multi-level IR with domain dialects. The closest existing technology to a biologically aware substrate, and the author's own preferred phrasing over 'a new BLAS'.

references.name: Chris Lattner
references.why: LLVM, Clang, MLIR, Swift. The central reference if the work genuinely enters dialects and domain-specific compilation.

references.name: Triton
references.why: The middle ground between high-level Python and hand-written CUDA — which is exactly where a semantic kernel would live.

references.name: Philippe Tillet
references.why: Author of Triton and of the paper behind it.

references.name: Apache TVM
references.why: How a high-level description becomes optimised code across different hardware — the same question in a different domain.

references.name: Tianqi Chen
references.why: TVM and machine-learning systems.

references.name: XLA
references.why: Tensor compilation and lowering; one of the systems the novelty claim has to be stated against rather than around.

references.name: IREE
references.why: MLIR-based lowering to multiple runtimes and hardware targets.

references.name: Halide
references.why: Separating WHAT to compute from HOW to compute it. The single most load-bearing idea under the semantic-kernel proposal: biological operation is not physical execution strategy.

references.name: TACO
references.why: Sparse tensor algebra compilation — where the SpGEMM line has to arrive once single-cell gains a time, patient or treatment axis.

references.name: Fredrik Kjolstad
references.why: TACO and sparse tensor compilation.

references.name: Differential dataflow
references.why: Incremental recomputation as data changes — the systems analogue of the thesis's G(t), a graph whose nodes and edges move.

references.name: Alan Turing — The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis (1952)
references.why: Global pattern from local rules. The author states the correct reading explicitly: this is NOT a claim that NF2 is a reaction-diffusion system.

references.name: Michael Levin
references.why: Bioelectricity, morphogenesis, collective cellular control — the contemporary reference closest to the author's curiosity about form and information in living systems.

references.name: Gunnar Carlsson
references.why: Topological data analysis.

references.name: Topological data analysis
references.why: Persistent homology and topological signatures over cell-state manifolds, tumour architecture and spatial data — to be reached for when there is a hypothesis, not for the mathematics.

references.name: Wolfram Physics Project
references.why: Adjacent influence on the complex-systems side; not a reference for NF2 and recorded as such.

references.name: Anton — D. E. Shaw Research
references.why: Special-purpose hardware for molecular dynamics. The historical proof of the principle the computational thesis rests on: when a domain matters enough, specialised hardware and software can beat general architectures by a lot.

references.name: David E. Shaw
references.why: Protein dynamics driven into specialised computation.

references.name: Folding@home
references.why: Distributed HPC applied to molecular biology — a different architecture for the same sampling problem.

authorFormula: Rare Disease + Systems Biology + Computational Biology + HPC + Compiler/Runtime Research — the author's own list of five. Complex systems and morphogenesis is carried here as a sixth, flagged as influence rather than as a discipline being bridged, because that is how the source material treats it.
finding: The comfortable reading of this map is that 7 of 10 rungs carry more than one community. The useful reading is the complement, and it is uncomfortable: 9 pairs of communities share no rung at all. Every one of those pairs has a biological community on one side and a computational one on the other. The high-performance-computing entries — 20 of them, the joint largest group here — sit entirely on the `substrate` rung, and no other community is on it. The compiler entries sit on `method` and meet only the complex-systems influences there. So the biological literatures and the computational literatures, in this map, never once talk about the same object.
theGap: This is the project's own central claim failing its own audit. The thesis says the unusual part is the intersection of rare disease, systems biology, computational biology, HPC and compiler research. The reference map says that intersection is currently EMPTY: the computational references are not references about biology, they are references about computation that the author intends to point at biology. That is a real and honourable position — it is what a research programme looks like before it has done the joining work — but it is not the same thing as a bridge, and the map is the wrong place to discover that after the thesis has been written. The rungs where the join would have to happen are `interactome`, `cell` and `tissue`: sparse graphs, sparse matrices and sparse neighbourhood tensors are all sitting there, and every reference at those rungs is biological.
